title: Respect: The Women of Rock and Soul
location: Brown County Playhouse, 70 S. Van Buren St, Nashville, IN, 47448, United States
description:
Jenn Cristy leads this vocal power-house show celebrating 60 years of women in music! Featuring the music of Aretha Franklin, Etta James, Whitney Houston, Tina Turner, The Supremes, Gladys Knight, Patti LaBelle, and Adele, just to name a few. This talented trio, including incredible vocalists Zoë Reed and Chrislyn Miller, gives the audience a concert experience with beautiful three-part harmonies and soaring renditions of both classic standards and popular music. This show will have you wanting more after every hit! Relive wonderful musical memories, while along with the Women of Rock and Soul we create brand new ones! It is a night to celebrate the women, the voices, the legends and the powerful impact they have made in history. 
Singer/songwriter Jenn Cristy has been refining her original sound for nearly a decade now as a solo artist, pushing in new directions with each album while always retaining the rock n’ roll soul that has brought audiences across the country to their feet. For the latest album, Crawl, Cristy spent nearly two years working with her band members before even entering the studio. The result is her most polished and nuanced album to date, a blend of storytelling lyrics with pop hooks and dazzling instrumental work that is sure to please both devoted fans and first-time listeners. Now on her fifth solo album, Jenn began her career with John Mellencamp, meeting the Hoosier rocker in Bloomington, Indiana, where she was in the midst of an all-American swimming career at Indiana University. During her stint with Mellencamp’s band she proved her versatility, playing flute, piano, percussion, organ, and violin in addition to singing. When she embarked on her solo career in 2003, she wanted to create a sound that both honored all of her varied influences – from Ben Folds to Pink and Bruce Hornsby to Queen – while creating something decidedly original. It is clear that her music has found a hungry audience. Cristy has played around the country, sharing the stage with a veritable who’s-who of artists – Shawn Mullins, John Eddie, Antigone Rising, Indigenous, Bree Sharp, Jeffery Gaines, Danielia Cotton and Michael Gabliki (Rusted Root) –or dominating it herself. Her songs have earned praise everywhere from blogs and small-town newspapers to The New York Times. The piano-driven rock is a platform for lyrics that encompass everything from matters of the heart to politics to straight-ahead fun…or murder. In Cristy’s world, every story has a melody.

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.

title: Lyle Lovett and his Small Large Band
description: A singer, composer and actor, Lyle Lovett has broadened the definition of American music in a career that spans 14 albums. Coupled with his gift for storytelling, the Texas-based musician fuses elements of country, swing, jazz, folk, gospel and blues in a convention-defying manner that breaks down barriers. Lovett’s live performances show not only the breadth of this Texas legend’s deep talents, but also the diversity of his influences, making him one of the most compelling and captivating musicians in popular music. Since his self-titled debut in 1986, Lyle Lovett has evolved into one of music’s most vibrant and iconic performers. Among his many accolades, besides the four Grammy Awards, he was given the Americana Music Association’s inaugural Trailblazer Award, and was named Texas State Musician. His works, rich and eclectic, are some of the most beloved of any artist working today.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.
source: IU Eskenazi School of Art, Architecture + Design

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Bloomington Libraries, IU Eskenazi School of Art

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s | Exhibition
description: Beth Battles (M.A. '26, Curatorship and B.A. '18, Fashion Design) investigated home sewing and the home sewing pattern industry in an Independent Study class and transformed her findings into a Curatorship capstone exhibition at IU Collections, A Stitch in Time: Home Sewing of the 1960s and 1970s. With guidance from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection, Beth selected 16 Sage Collection pieces to display on dress forms, accompanied by home sewing patterns, textbooks, and published materials. "A Stitch in Time" examines the home sewing industry's heyday in the 1960s and early 1970s that was fostered by simple pattern designs with fewer pieces reflective of the growing preference for looser, naturalistic silhouettes. Home sewing also empowered the home sewer to modify patterns to fit her body shape and aesthetic preferences.  While the Sage Collection at IU holds an incredible array of haute couture, historic fashion, and the Glenn Close Costume Collection, it is also a social history collection that includes everyday dress objects, such as jeans, T-shirts, tennis shoes, uniforms, and clothing sewn in the home from commercial patterns.McCalla summer operating hours:Wednesday-Friday May 20-June 26, 11:00 am-4:00 pm. Closed June 19 for the Juneteenth holiday and June 29-July 17.Reopening July 22, Wednesday-Friday, 11:00 am-4:00 pm for the rest of the summer until the Fall 2026 semester begins.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection
description: When Kripke died in 2020, she left behind a remarkable collection of over 20,000 dictionaries, as well as a rich manuscript archive about dictionaries, her life, and her collecting. In 2021, the Lilly Library acquired the collection, keeping it intact and available for all to study. The spring 2026 exhibition The Whole World in a Book: Celebrating Madeline Kripke's Dictionary Collection shares some of the collection publicly for the first time, curated by IU Provost Professor of English Michael Adams (https://english.indiana.edu/about/faculty/adams-michael.html) and Lilly Library Executive Associate Director Erika Dowell.  Madeline Kripke believed that dictionaries are an especially useful lens for observing culture. She focused on slang and other marginalized language, and she charted the roles of dictionaries in everyday life. She collected, not merely to possess, but to share what she saw with scholars and the public, and The Whole World in a Book realizes her ambition to do so.  This exhibition is on display until July 24, 2026. For the Lilly Library's daily hours, please visit the website (https://libraries.indiana.edu/lilly-library).

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: 15th Annual Indiana State Fingerstyle Guitar Festival
location: Brown County Playhouse, 70 S. Van Buren St, Nashville, IN, 47448, United States
description:
BUY TICKETS

The 15th Annual Indiana State Fingerstyle Guitar Festival features a morning guitar competition and an evening concert! Tickets are available separately for each, or an all-day pass is available. 
Fingerstyle Guitar Competition: 
11:00 AM – 2:00PM 
Acoustic guitarists from around the world take the stage for the 15th annual Fingerstyle Guitar Competition. The competition features two rounds of performance, showcasing a wide range of styles, techniques, and original music. At the conclusion of the competition, the top three players will be awarded grand-prize guitars and earn the honor of performing in the Evening Concert. 
Evening Concert: 
7:30 PM 
The Evening Concert features fingerstyle guitar legend Muriel Anderson, with special guests Tim Thompson and Jack Wilson. The concert will open with performances by the top three competition winners, giving audiences the chance to hear tomorrow’s guitar greats alongside established masters. 
Muriel Anderson is internationally celebrated for her mastery of the 20-string harp-guitar, her versatility across musical genres, and her warm, engaging stage presence. She was the first woman to win the National Fingerstyle Guitar Championship, and Guitar Player Magazine has named her one of the Top 50 Guitarists of All Time. Recently recognized among the Top Ten Female Guitarists, Muriel’s lasting legacy lies in her uplifting compositions and deeply expressive performances.
She has recorded with country legend Chet Atkins, performed with Les Paul and countless other greats in “Muriel Anderson’s All Star Guitar Night®” over the past 30+ years. Muriel’s CD Nightlight Daylight placed first in its category in 11 national awards, followed by Acoustic Chef, an international CD with cookbook. Muriel’s release Sailing Dreams exhibits new levels of creativity–she has even created a board game to accompany the music. 
Jack Wilson is a Chicagoland-based guitarist and 2013 Indiana Guitar Fest Champion. He won 1st place at the 2016 International Fingerstyle Guitar Competition at the Walnut Valley Festival after placing second in 2015. Appearing multiple times as a featured performer on our stage, Jack is a chameleon of a player, being able to shift comfortably from acoustic to electric, pick or fingerstyle in a wide range of styles, and immediately gets your attention by producing a cowbell sound from the guitar from his version of “Low Rider”. 
Tim Thompson is a Nashville-based fingerstyle guitarist and a two-time International Fingerstyle Guitar Champion. Long associated with our guitar festival, Tim’s career includes extensive session work and collaborations across genres, appearing with artists like Tommy Emmanuel, Crystal Gayle, and Hwy 101. He has recorded eleven CDs and two DVDs. He has been featured in the Taylor Guitar’s Wood and Steel, Just Jazz Guitar and Fingerstyle Guitar which said, “Tim Thompson is a Nashville based finger-stylist that burns!” 
Ticket Information 
Front & Center Tickets are limited to the first four rows in the center section of the theater and offer the closest possible view of the stage. 
BUY TICKETS

title: Hindley Street Country Club
description:
Founded in 2017 by arranger / producer Constantine Delo, The Hindley Street Country Club (The HSCC) started as a group of Adelaide (South Australia) musicians, recording re-arranged covers and uploading them weekly to Facebook and YouTube. Fast forward to today, The HSCC has amassed over 590 million YouTube views with over 1 million subscribers globally and accumulated over 1 billion views across social media platforms. Following on from major internet success, The HSCC now tours throughout the world.
The Hindley Street Country Club is making waves around the globe. With a strong foundation in Australia and neighbouring New Zealand, the band captivated audiences in Southeast Asia in 2024, performing at prestigious events like the Singapore Grand Prix and in vibrant Manila, Philippines. Early 2025 saw them embark on a dynamic tour across the United States and Brazil, showcasing their exceptional talent and energy. Now, they are gearing up for an exciting new national tour in the U.S., alongside a highly anticipated summer tour in Eastern Europe and stops in the United Kingdom.
Hindley Street is located in the centre of Adelaide, and many musicians who have played with HSCC had gigs in bands up and down that street in the 1970s, ‘80s and ‘90s. The name is a play on the reputation of the street, which, in addition to pubs, clubs, amusement arcades, cinemas, fast food outlets and ice cream parlours, featured adult entertainment, tattoo shops, motorcycle gangs and a steady stream of traffic cruising up and down the strip. Hindley Street is an eclectic mix of activity today, including a university campus at one end. There is no actual ‘country club’ on Hindley Street in Adelaide, and the in-joke is mixing up a genteel concept like a country club with ‘Hindley Street.’

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.

title: I Ride
location: Sherwood Oaks Christian Church, 2700 E Rogers Rd, Bloomington, IN 47401, USA
description:
The iRide is a no drop ride with regroup points geared toward the rider wanting to push the pace a bit without being race oriented. 16-18mph avg on most rides. title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.

location: Redbud Books, 408 W Kirkwood Ave, Bloomington, IN 47404, USA
description:
A long-term, hybrid in-person and online reading group in memory of our beloved friend, Joshua Clover inspired by Joshua’s understanding of communism, and social transformation. 

Our itinerary begins with Riot Strike Riot (Clover) and works backward through Chaos and Governance in the Modern World System (Arrighi and silver ), The Eclipse And Re-emergence Of The Communist Movement(Dauvé and Martin), The Arcana Of Reproduction (Fortunati, Trans Austin and Colantuono), Notes On Dialectics (James), Capital V I (Marx, Trans Reitter or Fowkes) and then returns to the present for The Future of Revolution (Bernes). 

If people agree the group will be run as a discussion by rotating facilitators. It could last 18 months or so.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.

location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Step into the world of acclaimed photographer Rania Matar (b. 1964, Lebanon), whose striking portraits document young women persisting in uncertain times. Matar's lens highlights women's creativity, strength, dignity, and resilience—offering a powerful counter-narrative to the challenges of her country and region. Read more about this featured exhibition (https://artmuseum.indiana.edu/exhibitions/upcoming/_feature-exhibitions/2026-03-05-rania-matar-where-do-i-go.html).  Join us for a rare opportunity to explore the artist's work in depth, guided by the scholar who researched and curated the exhibition. Read Leila Reichert's bio. (http://Elliot%20Josephine%20Leila%20Reichert%20is%20an%20American%20curator,%20critic,%20and%20editor.%20She%20is%20the%20inaugural%20Curator%20of%20Contemporary%20Art%20at%20the%20Eskenazi%20Museum%20of%20Art%20at%20Indiana%20University%20and%20was%20a%202023-24%20Propel%20Fellow%20with%20the%20Association%20of%20Art%20Museum%20Curators%20Foundation.%20She%20was%20formerly%20Art%20Editor%20of%20Newcity%20and%20Assistant%20Curator%20at%20the%20Block%20Museum%20of%20Art,%20Northwestern%20University.%20She%20has%20curated%20and%20assisted%20in%20developing%20critically%20celebrated%20exhibitions%20in%20the%20United%20States%20and%20abroad.%20Her%20critical%20writing%20has%20been%20published%20in%20the%20Journal%20of%20Visual%20Studies,%20Hyperallergic,%20the%20Brooklyn%20Rail,%20Newcity%20Art,%20and%20The%20Seen,%20among%20others.%20She%20holds%20dual%20masters%E2%80%99%20degrees%20in%20Modern%20and%20Contemporary%20Art%20History%20and%20Arts%20Administration%20and%20Cultural%20Policy%20from%20the%20School%20of%20the%20Art%20Institute%20of%20Chicago%20and%20a%20Bachelors%20of%20Arts%20with%20Honors%20in%20Art%20History%20from%20Northwestern%20University,%20where%20she%20graduated%20summa%20cum%20laude.)  Reserve your spot today for a chance to connect with Rania Matar's striking photographs in a personal, meaningful way. Leila will share the stories, research, and insights behind the exhibition, making this experience as memorable as the photography itself.Know Before You GoSpace is limited to 15 participants. RSVP to reserve a space. Walk-ins are welcome if space is available. If this page says "registration has closed", this means that registration and the waitlist have filled for this date and time.Plan to arrive early to check in. At 1:25 p.m., any unclaimed spaces may be released to guests who are standing by waiting for a space.Admission and tours are free.A small handbag may be carried at your side. Larger bags and backpacks will need to be stored before touring.Read about where to find us, where to park, accessibility, and museum guidelines.When You ArriveCheck in with Guest Services staff on the first floor.If you park in the IMU parking lot, Guest Services can validate your parking voucher for a discount.Be sure to store backpacks and large bags before touring. Lockers and coat racks are available.Keep space (18") between yourself, including anything you're carrying, and the art.

title: Beginner/Intermediate Drawing Workshop
location: SIDNEY AND LOIS ESKENAZI MUSEUM OF ART
description: Reserve your spot. If this page says, "Registration has closed" that means the waitlist is full.SuppliesBring your favorite drawing pencil (e.g. 4B), a sketchbook or drawing paper, and a phone or device to photograph artwork (without flash) as we sketch.  Know Before You GoArrive early to find parking, check in, and get your drawing supplies ready.  At 1:55 p.m. any unclaimed reservations will be released to guests who are standing by waiting for a spot.  Where to find us, where to park, accessibility, and museum guidelines (https://artmuseum.indiana.edu/visit/your-visit.html).  This workshop is recommended for ages 12 and up. Anyone under 18, who is not an IU student, must be accompanied by an adult.  When You ArriveCheck in with Guest Services at the information desk on the first floor, even if you come often and even if you are late. We appreciate having an accurate attendance count.  Store all backpacks and large bags before entering the galleries. A small handbag may be carried at your side.  Get your supplies ready. Attach an 18x24" piece of newsprint to a drawing board.  Cancellations  This workshop often has a waitlist. Please use the cancellation link included with your confirmation email if your plans change.About the Instructor  John Cheek has taught credit and non-credit classes for eight years in portrait painting, landscape painting, palette knife painting, life drawing, beginning drawing, and advanced drawing, as well as in design. He volunteers his time and expertise to facilitate drawing workshops at the Eskenazi Museum of Art.

description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Bloomington Libraries, IU Eskenazi School of Art

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

description:
Every Wednesday at 8PM is Comedy Attic Open Mic Night. Bloomington has one of the best local comedy scenes in the country, and it all starts with our open mic night!

Each comedian is asked to do no more than five minutes of completely original material. While we do not care about foul language in your set, we do not allow racist, homophobic, transphobic or rape/female bashing jokes. If you have to ask if it's racist, homophobic, transphobic or a rape joke, it probably is.

Comedians that wish to participate are asked to e-mail comedyattic@gmail.com mailto:comedyattic@gmail.com . Newcomers and any participants who are not paid professionals will be required to bring audience members to see them. This is non-negotiable. So if you plan on signing up, be sure to invite as many friends as you can. Good luck!

title: Materialism Reading Group
location: Redbud Books, 408 W Kirkwood Ave, Bloomington, IN 47404, USA
description:
A long-term, hybrid in-person and online reading group in memory of our beloved friend, Joshua Clover inspired by Joshua’s understanding of communism, and social transformation. 

Our itinerary begins with Riot Strike Riot (Clover) and works backward through Chaos and Governance in the Modern World System (Arrighi and silver ), The Eclipse And Re-emergence Of The Communist Movement(Dauvé and Martin), The Arcana Of Reproduction (Fortunati, Trans Austin and Colantuono), Notes On Dialectics (James), Capital V I (Marx, Trans Reitter or Fowkes) and then returns to the present for The Future of Revolution (Bernes). 

If people agree the group will be run as a discussion by rotating facilitators. It could last 18 months or so.

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.
source: IU Arts & Humanities Institute, IU Bloomington Libraries

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.

title: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, the Moment
description: The Declaration of Independence: The Motives, The Momentexamines a crucial time in American history through the collections of the Lilly Library. The first printing of the Declaration of Independence, one of only twenty-six copies known today, is the centerpiece of the exhibition. Printed immediately for distribution, it is the source of all revolutionary era reprintings. The famous hand-written version was an official formality created later, signed in August, and stored away.Books, pamphlets, newspapers, prints, and letters allow viewers to explore key questions about this moment in time. How did a people proud to be in the British empire come to believe independence was possible or even desirable? What ideas and historical events did they draw on to justify resistance to Great Britain? What kinds of communication networks would be crucial for circulating the Declaration and countless other revolutionary documents throughout the colonies?This exhibition is part of America 250 at IU (https://go.iu.edu/america-250), a months-long civic festival offering our state expansive programming, exhibits, and events to honor our country's past while looking toward our shared future through common experiences for our campus and community.

description:
The Community Bike Project is a Bloomington-based organization that focuses on providing bike transportation to the people of the city. We focus on teaching bicycle maintenence in order to ensure that bikes on the streets stay on the streets. Here is what we do: Community Bike Project Front Door



    * bikes for sale: we sell gently used bikes at bargain prices

description:
Audition Notice: 
Arsenic and Old Lace
by Joseph Kesselring 
Save the date!! Arsenic and Old Lace auditions at the Brown County Playhouse. 
Audition Notice: The Brown County Playhouse and director Susan Rardin, will hold auditions for Arsenic and Old Lace on Monday, August 10th and Tuesday, August 11th at 7pm. Auditions will be held at the Brown County Playhouse. Sides will be available for perusal at 6:30pm each night. Production dates are October 2, 3, 4, 9, 10. Rehearsals will be four evenings per week with rehearsals starting Sunday August 16th. Contact Susan Rardin, if questions. 
Show synopsis: Drama critic Mortimer Brewster’s engagement announcement is upended when he discovers a corpse in his elderly aunts’ window seat. Mortimer rushes to tell Abby and Martha before they stumble upon the body themselves, only to learn that the two old women aren’t just aware of the dead man in their parlor, they killed him! Between his aunts’ penchant for poisoning wine, a brother who thinks he’s Teddy Roosevelt, and another brother using plastic surgery to hide from the police – not to mention Mortimer’s own hesitancy about marriage – it’ll be a miracle if Mortimer makes it to his wedding. Arsenic and Old Lace is a classic dark comedy about the only thing more deadly than poison: family. 
  
The following roles are needed: 
Abby Brewster: (stage age 65-80) One of the Brewster sisters who reside in the family home. 
Martha Brewster: (stage age 65-80) One of the Brewster sisters who reside in the family home. 
Jonathan Brewster: (Stage age 45-60) Eldest nephew of the Brewster sisters. A criminal and murderer on the lam. Sinister, threatening, imposing. His face has been surgically transformed to look like Boris Karloff. 
Dr. Einstein: (Stage age 35-70) Jonathan’s criminal partner. He is responsible forJonathan’s facial transformation. 
Teddy Brewster: (Stage age 40-65) Middle nephew of the Brewster sisters. Believes he is Teddy Roosevelt. Jovial and good-natured. 
Mortimer Brewster: (Stage Age 25-45) Youngest nephew of the Brewster sisters. In love with Elaine Harper. Works for the newspaper reviewing plays. Kind 
and funny. Is doted on by his aunts. 
Elaine Harper: (Stage age 25-40) Girlfriend of Mortimer. Daughter of the Rev. Dr. Harper. 
Reverend Dr. Harper: (Stage age 50-70) Minister of nearby church. Neighbor of the Brewsters. Father of Elaine. 
Officer Brophy: (Stage age 25-60) Brooklyn police officer. 
Officer Klein: (Stage age 20-50) Brooklyn police officer. 
Officer O’Hara: (Stage age 30-50) Brooklyn police officer. Aspires to be a playwright. 
Lieutenant Rooney: (Stage age 50-70) Brooklyn police Lieutenant. Senior officer. 
Mr. Gibbs (Stage age 65-80) Potential boarder. 
Mr. Witherspoon: (Stage age 60-80) Superintendent of the local looney bin.

title: Louisa's Garden | Exhibition
description: Louisa's Garden, the Wylie House Museum's latest exhibition, explores the way the eldest daughter of an IU professor was brave, complex, and is still cherished today. For Louisa's Garden, Graduate Curatorship student Maddie Guy selected five ensembles from the Elizabeth Sage Historic Costume Collection. These five nineteenth century ensembles, though not directly related to Louisa Wylie Boisen (1839–1930), were carefully chosen to represent aspects of her life including Education, Motherhood, Travel, Religion, and Gardening.Wylie House hours: Friday–Saturday, 10am–4pm. Free, guided tours begin on the hour every hour, with the last one beginning at 3pm. The museum is closed on major holidays, IU commencement weekend, and during Indiana University breaks. Please contact the museum to arrange group tours with more than eight people.  For more information about The Sage Collection, please visit their webpage. (https://eskenazi.indiana.edu/about/centers-collections/sage-collection/index.html)  For more information about Wylie House Museum (https://libraries.indiana.edu/wylie-house-museum) visit their website.
source: Architecture + Design, IU Bloomington Libraries, IU Eskenazi School of Art

title: Micro-mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature
description: "Myths are the world's dreams."- Joseph Campbell.To believe is to be human.One of the greatest forces known to humankind,belief is a universal impetus, one that has raised and toppled temples, instigated and eased wars, and inspired written works, both monumental and miniature. This exhibition showcases a selection of minute materials that pertain to mythologies and belief systems from across the world. From ancient Mesopotamian myth to modern Native American spirituality, belief transcends time and history and intertwines human existence within our world.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is a miniature book exhibition which seeks to highlight some of our oldest and most powerful stories, as well as those who preserved them.Mythological influence has shaped the world around us. Whether that be through architecture, art, or literature, myths serve as a testament to human cultural memory and the preservation of intangible tradition. Myths pull back the curtain of the past and reunite us with the beliefs and stories of our ancestors.Most of these materials originate from the collection of prolific miniature book collector, Ruth Elizabeth Adomeit (1910-1996). Notable book artists highlighted inMicro-Mythologies include Maryline Poole Adams, Carol Cunningham, Barbara J. Raheb, Dianne Weiss, and Gabrielle Fox.Micro-Mythologies: World Mythology Made Miniature is curated by Curatorial Assistant Jake Gentry, with counsel from Sarah McElroy Mitchell, Curator of Religious Collections. In addition, exhibition design was done by Jenny Mack and graphic design by David Orr. This exhibition is on display in the Lilly Library Ball Room through December 2026.
